content.question: What does `.text` do when called on an EditText variable in Kotlin?

It deletes the text from the EditText
It changes the hint of the EditText
It hides the EditText from the screen

content.question: Why do we call `.toString()` after `.text` when collecting input from an EditText?

To convert it into an Integer
To display it on screen automatically
To encrypt the text for security

content.question: What is the correct order of operations when collecting text from an EditText in Kotlin?

Demand text → call the component → convert to string
Call the component → convert to string → demand text

content.question: What is a Toast message in Android?

A permanent text label on the screen

A notification in the status bar

content.question: What is the correct syntax for creating a Toast message in Kotlin?

`Toast.create(this, "message").display()`
`Toast.show("message")`
`makeToast(this, "message")`

content.explanation: Toast.makeText() creates the toast with context (`this`), the message text, and duration. `.show()` is required to actually display it on screen.

content.question: Why was using two separate if-else blocks (one for username, one for password) considered problematic?

options.text: The code becomes bulky and messy with too many if-else statements
Kotlin does not allow two if-else blocks
It causes the app to crash
It makes the Toast messages disappear

content.explanation: Having separate if-else blocks for each credential check makes the code bulky and harder to maintain. A single combined condition using a logical operator is cleaner.

content.question: What is the logical AND operator (`&&`) used for in Kotlin?

options.text: To check if BOTH conditions are true simultaneously
To check if at least one condition is true
To negate a condition
To assign values to two variables at once

content.explanation: The `&&` (AND) operator combines two conditions. Both must be true for the overall result to be true. If either is false, the result is false.

content.question: Using `&&`, what happens if the username is correct but the password is wrong?

options.text: The overall condition is false and the else block executes
The if block still executes because one condition is true
Only the username check passes and a partial login occurs
The app crashes due to mismatched conditions

content.explanation: With `&&`, BOTH conditions must be true. If even one condition (password check) is false, the entire if condition becomes false and the else block runs.
hints: AND requires both to be true
One false makes the whole thing false

content.question: What is the correct syntax for combining username and password checks using the AND operator?

options.text: `if ((username == userId) && (password == userPassword))`
`if (username == userId AND password == userPassword)`
`if (username && password == userId && userPassword)`
`if (username == userId) && if (password == userPassword)`

content.explanation: Each condition is wrapped in parentheses and connected with `&&`. Both conditions are placed inside a single if statement's parentheses.
hints: Each condition gets its own parentheses

content.question: In the AND truth table, what result do you get when Condition A is true and Condition B is false?

options.text: false
true
null
Error

content.explanation: With the AND operator, if any one condition is false, the entire result is false. Both A and B must be true to get true.

Think of a gate that needs both keys

content.question: What advantage does using `&&` in a single if-else give over using two separate if-else blocks?

options.text: Reduces code, avoids repetition, and checks both conditions in one statement
It runs faster because it uses less memory
It allows checking more than two conditions only
It automatically handles null values

content.explanation: Using `&&` combines both checks into one if statement, eliminating duplicate if-else blocks and making the code cleaner and less bulky.
